I have a gallon of honey and a gallon of mayonnaise at 25C. I remove one cup of honey at a time from the gallon of honey. How many times will I need to remove a cup to have the honey weigh less than the mayonaise? Assume the containers themselves weigh the same.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Found Chemistry LibreTexts page "1.7: Density" with a table of common substance densities at 25°C. The table lists:
- mayonnaise: 0.910 g/cm^3
- honey: 1.420 g/cm^3
The page shows contributors Marisa Alviar-Agnew and Henry Agnew and is within the Introductory/CK-12-aligned materials. URL: https://chem.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Introductory_Chemistry/Chemistry_for_Changing_Times_(Hill_and_McCreary)/01:_Chemistry/1.07:_Density
These appear to be the requested CK-12 densities at 25°C.

history.name: Assistant
history.content:
Using CK-12/LibreTexts densities: honey 1.420 g/mL, mayonnaise 0.910 g/mL. Standard volumes: 1 gallon = 16 cups; 1 cup = 236.588 mL; so 1 gallon = 16 × 236.588 = 3785.408 mL.
- Mass of a gallon of honey = 1.420 × 3785.408 ≈ 5375.3 g.
- Mass of a gallon of mayonnaise = 0.910 × 3785.408 ≈ 3445.7 g.
Each cup of honey removed has mass 1.420 × 236.588 ≈ 336.0 g.
Let n cups be removed. Remaining honey mass = 5375.3 − 336.0 n. Require 5375.3 − 336.0 n < 3445.7 ⇒ 1929.6 < 336.0 n ⇒ n > 5.74 ⇒ minimum n = 6.
Preliminary result: 6 cups. I can proceed to present or we can verify the exact source metadata as requested.
